abstract: RNA polymerase II often starts transcription inside genes, usually at elements that initiate in both directions. An intragenic start pointing in the gene's direction (a sense start) makes RNA that passes the gene's splice sites and polyadenylation signals and may interfere with the gene. Introns may therefore have lost sequences that start sense transcription. In PRO-cap data from K562 and HCT116 cells, the sense start at intronic elements, measured against the antisense start, is a fifth to a third weaker than at intergenic elements of similar read depth. Sequence models that have never seen an element's chromosome predict 30-42% of this bias from local DNA, except models trained on K562 applied to HCT116. However, introns as a whole show little or no depletion of predicted sense starts, and among 76,215 human genomes, variants predicted to create sense starts are not kept rarer than those creating antisense starts. In both cell lines, and in K562 GRO-cap data, strong measured start sites are rarer on the gene strand, mainly near the 5'' end of active genes. Thus, weaker sense starts appear to be a feature of individual active elements, partly predictable from their sequence, and we find no sign that selection has removed such sequences from introns.
